title: Divisibility of $J(C)(k)$ and the $n$-torsion of $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$
statement:
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $C/k$ be a smooth proper connected
curve of genus $g$, with Jacobian $J(C)$.

1. For every $n\ge1$, multiplication by $n$ on $J(C)(k)$ is surjective.
2. Let $n>0$. The inclusion $J(C)(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\subset\operatorname{Pic}(C)$
   restricts to an equality
   $$
   J(C)[n](k)=J(C)(k)[n]=\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n],
   $$
   and the degree map induces an isomorphism
   $$
   \operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow[\ \deg\ ]{\sim}\Z/n\Z.
   $$

proof.text: Put $J=J(C)$ and write the Picard group additively. By [sk-thm-picard-main], $J$ is an abelian variety and the identification $J(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$ is an identification of groups. By [lem-sc-pic-proper-decomposition], the degree is a surjective group homomorphism and its kernel is exactly $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$. Thus, identifying $J(k)$ with its image, we have the short exact sequence $0\to J(k)\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow{\deg}\mathbf Z\to0$. The hypotheses of both statements are precisely that $k$ is algebraically closed and $C$ is a smooth proper connected curve.

Fix any $n\ge1$. Apply [lem-sc-isogeny-surjective] to the abelian variety $J$ from step 1: for every $y\in J(k)$ there is $x\in J(k)$ with $nx=y$. This proves (1), and in particular $nJ(k)=J(k)$. This lemma requires only $n\ge1$, including when the characteristic divides $n$; its surjectivity is the finite-surjective-fibre argument referred to in the blueprint.

By [sk-def-av-mult-n], $J[n]=J\times_{[n],J,e}\operatorname{Spec}k$. A $k$-point of this fibre product is uniquely a point $a\in J(k)$ satisfying $na=0$, so $J[n](k)=J(k)[n]$. If $L\in\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ satisfies $nL=0$, the degree homomorphism in step 1 gives $n\deg L=0$ in $\mathbf Z$. Since $n>0$, this forces $\deg L=0$. Exactness therefore puts $L$ in $J(k)$, and its same equation says $L\in J(k)[n]$. Conversely, the inclusion of this subgroup into $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ preserves $nL=0$. Hence the inclusion restricts to the asserted equality of torsion subgroups.

source.place: (2), kernel identity and torsion part of the multiplication-by-n diagram

proof.text: Degree induces a homomorphism $\overline{\deg}:\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)\to\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z$: replacing $L$ by $L+nM$ changes its degree by $n\deg M$. It is surjective because the degree homomorphism is surjective by [lem-sc-pic-proper-decomposition]: for an integer representative $d$ choose $L$ of degree $d$, whose class maps to $d\bmod n$.

source.place: (2), cokernel part of the multiplication-by-n diagram: induced degree and surjectivity

proof.text: For injectivity let $L$ represent a class in the kernel of $\overline{\deg}$. Then $\deg L=nm$ for some $m\in\mathbf Z$. By [lem-sc-pic-proper-decomposition] choose $M\in\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ with $\deg M=m$. The element $L-nM$ has degree zero, hence belongs to $J(k)$ by step 1. By step 2 choose $B\in J(k)$ with $nB=L-nM$. Inside the Picard group this gives $L=n(M+B)$, so the original quotient class is zero. Thus $\overline{\deg}$ is injective as well as surjective. Its inverse is additive: the preimages of a sum and the sum of the preimages have the same image and hence coincide by injectivity. This is the claimed isomorphism induced by degree.
